The normalized IMEP distributions exhibited narrow standard deviations comparable to baseline operation, confirming that the introduction of the reformed fuel did not increase cycle-to-cycle variability. This stability suggests that the hydrogen and short-chain hydrocarbon components promote faster and more reliable ignition even at slightly lower total fuel energy. The consistency of these results across multiple plasma duty cycles demonstrates that the reformer provided a steady, homogeneous reformate composition under all tested conditions. The observed reduction in methane leaks under high-speed operation, particularly in the Cummins X15N engine, further highlights the kinetic benefits of plasma reforming. Engines operating at elevated speeds have shorter residence times and greater turbulence, which enhance the mixing and chemical utilization of hydrogen and acetylene. Under these conditions, plasma-generated intermediates accelerate oxidation reactions that would otherwise be kinetically limited in a purely methane-fueled system. In contrast, the effect was more modest in lower-speed engines such as the AJAX 2802, where reformed fuel was integrated into the pre- chambers. However, the measurable improvements still demonstrated that the reformer provides benefits across a range of combustion regimes. From an energy perspective, the plasma reformer demonstrated a low energy consumption that achieved the project target of less than one percent of engine output. During plasma-assisted operation on the Cummins X15N engine, the fuel’s effective lower heating value decreased by an estimated 3–7 percent as carbon was removed from the gas stream at increasing plasma duty cycles. Measured reductions in gIMEP (3–6 percent) and peak heat-release rate (4–6 percent) tracked this decrease within experimental scatter. The proportional relationship between input- energy reduction (ΔLHV) and output-work reduction (ΔIMEP, ΔHRR) indicates that the engine’s overall thermodynamic efficiency remained essentially unchanged, confirming that the reformer’s impact on system efficiency was minimal. By converting only a small fraction of the incoming fuel to reactive species, the system achieves a meaningful reduction in methane leaks without materially affecting total engine performance or power balance. Beyond its direct exhaust-control function, plasma reforming also offers potential benefits for combustion durability and control. The smoother pressure rise and reduced thermal gradients observed during plasma-assisted operation suggest a more uniform temperature field within the combustion chamber, which could reduce mechanical stress on engine components and extend service life. Although EMI is an inherent characteristic of high-voltage pulsed plasma systems, appropriate shielding and grounding effectively mitigated its impact. Once these controls were implemented, EMI did not significantly affect engine sensors or control performance, demonstrating that the technology can be integrated with modern engine-management systems without adverse effects. Taken together, these findings indicate that plasma fuel reforming can enhance oxidation completeness and reduce methane slip by simultaneously enriching the fuel stream with reactive species and moderating total heat release. The process produces a more stable and energy- efficient combustion environment without exceeding practical power or thermal limits.
